entry.title: Can You Earn Money From GitHub? Yes — Here’s How

link.title: Can You Earn Money From GitHub? Yes — Here’s How

entry.content:
Can you earn money from GitHub?

Yes. Developers earn money from GitHub in several ways, from a few dollars a month to full-time income, and it doesn’t require building the next big framework. Some maintainers earn through recurring sponsorships, others get paid per pull request through bounties, and many use their GitHub activity to land consulting work.

5 ways developers earn money on GitHub

  • GitHub Sponsors — recurring payments from the community or companies that depend on your work
  • Paid issues / bounties — a sponsor attaches a price to an issue, a contributor submits a PR, and payment is released on merge
  • Consulting and support — companies using your project pay for setup help, custom features, or priority support
  • Company-funded maintenance — a business that depends on your repository funds ongoing work or sponsors specific features
  • Freelance work sourced from GitHub — your public contributions act as a portfolio that leads to paid client work

Why bounties are the fastest way to start

Bounty amounts vary by scope:

  • Micro-fixes and small bugs: $20–$200
  • Feature-level work and integrations: $200–$2,500
  • Major features or architecture changes: $2,500–$25,000

Unlike sponsorships, which build slowly, a bounty pays for a single, well-defined piece of work you can complete this week.

The problem with informal GitHub bounties

Plenty of maintainers already offer to “pay for a PR” in an issue comment, but informal bounties have real friction:

  • No escrow, so contributors work on trust alone
  • No clear process for who gets paid if two people submit a fix
  • Payment depends on the maintainer remembering to follow up
  • Cross-border payments add fees and delays

How Gitpay turns GitHub issues into paid bounties

Gitpay connects sponsors, maintainers, and contributors directly on top of your existing GitHub workflow:

  1. A sponsor or maintainer opens (or imports) a GitHub issue and funds it as a task
  2. Contributors browse open tasks and apply to work on the one that fits
  3. The contributor submits a Pull Request against the issue
  4. Once the PR is merged, the contributor requests payment and gets paid

No spreadsheets, no chasing payments in DMs — the bounty, the PR, and the payout are tied to the same issue from start to finish.

Example use cases

  • A maintainer funds a backlog of “help wanted” issues to speed up development
  • A company sponsors a feature it needs in a dependency it doesn’t maintain
  • A contributor builds a track record (and income) by working through funded issues across multiple repositories
  • A freelance developer uses funded issues as steady, low-friction project work between clients

Getting started

  • Want to earn? Browse funded issues, apply, submit a PR, and request payment when it’s merged.
  • Want to fund work? Turn a GitHub issue into a task, set a bounty, and release payment once the PR is delivered.

Using Gitpay

Gitpay is the open source platform for funding and getting paid for GitHub issues:

  • https://gitpay.me

CTA

Yes, you can earn money from GitHub. Start with a funded issue: https://gitpay.me
entry.summary: Yes, you can earn money from GitHub: GitHub Sponsors, paid issues, consulting, and bounties. See how Gitpay turns GitHub issues into paid bounties you can fund or work on.

entry.title: Dá para Ganhar Dinheiro no GitHub? Sim — Veja Como

link.title: Dá para Ganhar Dinheiro no GitHub? Sim — Veja Como

entry.content:
Dá para ganhar dinheiro no GitHub?

Sim. Desenvolvedores ganham dinheiro no GitHub de várias formas, de alguns dólares por mês a uma renda em tempo integral, e isso não exige criar o próximo grande framework. Alguns mantenedores ganham com patrocínios recorrentes, outros recebem por Pull Request através de bounties, e muitos usam sua atividade no GitHub para conseguir trabalhos de consultoria.

5 formas de ganhar dinheiro no GitHub

  • GitHub Sponsors — pagamentos recorrentes da comunidade ou de empresas que dependem do seu trabalho
  • Issues pagas / bounties — um patrocinador define um valor para uma issue, um contribuidor envia um PR, e o pagamento é liberado quando o PR é aceito
  • Consultoria e suporte — empresas que usam seu projeto pagam por ajuda na configuração, funcionalidades sob medida ou suporte prioritário
  • Manutenção financiada por empresas — uma empresa que depende do seu repositório financia trabalho contínuo ou patrocina funcionalidades específicas
  • Trabalho freelance originado no GitHub — suas contribuições públicas funcionam como portfólio e geram trabalho remunerado com clientes

Por que bounties são a forma mais rápida de começar

Os valores de bounties variam conforme o escopo:

  • Correções pequenas e bugs simples: US$ 20–US$ 200
  • Funcionalidades e integrações: US$ 200–US$ 2.500
  • Funcionalidades grandes ou mudanças de arquitetura: US$ 2.500–US$ 25.000

Diferente do patrocínio, que cresce devagar, uma bounty paga por um trabalho único e bem definido que você pode entregar em uma semana.

O problema das bounties informais no GitHub

Muitos mantenedores já oferecem “pago por um PR” em um comentário de issue, mas bounties informais têm atrito real:

  • Não há garantia de pagamento (escrow), então o contribuidor trabalha na confiança
  • Não há processo claro para definir quem recebe se duas pessoas enviarem a correção
  • O pagamento depende do mantenedor lembrar de dar retorno
  • Pagamentos internacionais somam taxas e atrasos

Como o Gitpay transforma issues do GitHub em bounties pagas

O Gitpay conecta patrocinadores, mantenedores e contribuidores diretamente sobre o seu fluxo de trabalho no GitHub:

  1. Um patrocinador ou mantenedor abre (ou importa) uma issue do GitHub e a financia como uma tarefa
  2. Contribuidores navegam pelas tarefas disponíveis e se candidatam para a que combina com eles
  3. O contribuidor envia um Pull Request referente à issue
  4. Depois que o PR é aceito, o contribuidor solicita o pagamento e recebe

Sem planilhas, sem cobrar pagamento no direct — a bounty, o PR e o pagamento ficam ligados à mesma issue do início ao fim.

Exemplos de uso

  • Um mantenedor financia um backlog de issues “help wanted” para acelerar o desenvolvimento
  • Uma empresa patrocina uma funcionalidade que precisa em uma dependência que não mantém
  • Um contribuidor constrói histórico (e renda) trabalhando em issues financiadas em vários repositórios
  • Um desenvolvedor freelancer usa issues financiadas como trabalho constante e de baixo atrito entre clientes

Como começar

  • Quer ganhar? Veja as issues financiadas, candidate-se, envie um PR e solicite o pagamento quando ele for aceito.
  • Quer financiar trabalho? Transforme uma issue do GitHub em tarefa, defina uma bounty e libere o pagamento quando o PR for entregue.

Usando o Gitpay

O Gitpay é a plataforma open source para financiar e receber por issues do GitHub:

  • https://gitpay.me

CTA

Sim, dá para ganhar dinheiro no GitHub. Comece com uma issue financiada: https://gitpay.me

entry.title: How to Request Payment After Delivering Software Work

link.title: How to Request Payment After Delivering Software Work

entry.content:
The problem: the work is done, and now you wait

You merged the PR. You deployed it. The feature works. And now you’re in the part of the job nobody talks about at meetups: waiting to get paid.

Sometimes the wait is a formal invoice sitting in an accounts-payable queue. Sometimes it’s a GitHub issue with a bounty attached and no clear next step once the pull request lands. Either way, the gap between “the code is done” and “the money is in my account” is where most freelance developers and open-source contributors lose time and patience.

This article walks through two related situations — because “software work” covers both:

  1. You did freelance or contract work for a client and need to collect payment for a deliverable.
  2. You did the work by fixing a GitHub issue that had a bounty attached, and need the bounty released after your pull request is merged.

Both end the same way: money moving from the person who wanted the work done to the person who did it. The path there is different enough to cover separately.

Payment request vs. invoice

A quick definition, since the two get used interchangeably and shouldn’t be:

  • An invoice is a formal billing document: it states what was provided, the amount owed, and payment terms, and is usually the record a client’s finance team files for accounting or tax purposes.
  • A payment request is an action, not a document: a link that lets the payer pay you online, right now, for a specific amount. It doesn’t replace the accounting record a client’s finance team might still need — it replaces the friction of getting from “work is done” to “money moved.”

This isn’t legal or tax advice — whether you also need to issue a formal invoice depends on your business setup, your client’s requirements, and your local rules. A payment request is about removing the operational lag between delivery and payment; it doesn’t decide your tax obligations for you.

Situation 1: freelance or contract delivery

The usual failure mode

Most freelance payment delays follow the same pattern:

  • You finish the work and hand it off.
  • You send an invoice, or you’re told to submit one to a portal.
  • The invoice sits in a queue — waiting for approval, waiting for a monthly payment run, or waiting for someone in finance to notice it.
  • You follow up. Maybe twice.

None of this is really about trust or amount. It’s about the payment step requiring more effort than paying for a SaaS subscription does.

A concrete example

Say you’re a freelance developer who just shipped a scoped piece of work: “Add Stripe checkout, webhook handling, and receipt emails” for a client’s app.

  1. You merge the PR and deploy to production.
  2. You write a short handoff message: what changed, where it’s live, how to verify it.
  3. In the same message, you include a payment request link for the agreed amount.

That third step is the one people skip, and it’s the one that matters most. If the payment request isn’t in the same message as the handoff, payment becomes a separate task the client has to remember to come back to — and “I’ll deal with it later” is where invoices go to die.

When to send the request

Two timing patterns work in practice:

  • Milestone-based — right after a merged, deployed milestone.
  • Cycle-based — at the end of an agreed period, e.g. “hours worked this week.”

Don’t send it before you can say “done” with confidence, and don’t wait until the client has mentally moved on to the next priority. The window is short.

If the client still needs a formal invoice

Some clients’ finance departments require one regardless of how they pay. That’s fine — the payment request is the “pay now” action; a formal invoice can still follow (or be attached) for their records. You’re not choosing one over the other; the payment request just stops the invoice from being the only path to getting paid.

Situation 2: getting paid for a bounty-funded GitHub issue

This is a different shape of the same problem, common on Gitpay and similar platforms.

The workflow

  1. A sponsor or maintainer funds a GitHub issue with a bounty amount.
  2. A contributor claims the task — this confirms they’re the GitHub user assigned to work on it, so the bounty is reserved for them rather than up for grabs by anyone.
  3. The contributor delivers the work as a pull request, following whatever review process the repository uses (tests, CI checks, maintainer review).
  4. Once the maintainer accepts the PR — typically once it’s merged — the bounty is released.
  5. The payment shows up as a transfer to the contributor’s account, which they then withdraw as a payout.

The pull request is doing the same job the “handoff message” did in the freelance example: it’s the concrete, reviewable artifact that acceptance is based on. No PR (or equivalent accepted deliverable), no clear moment to release payment.

Why “claim first” matters

Skipping the claim step and just opening a PR against an open bounty is a common mistake. Without an explicit claim, you risk duplicating effort with someone else already working on it, or building against a scope that shifted after you started. Claiming first is what gives you (and the maintainer) a shared, agreed starting point.

What happens if nobody delivers

Bounty-funded issues don’t stay in limbo forever. If a task goes unclaimed for a long stretch, most platforms — Gitpay included — periodically check in and eventually release the task back to be claimed by someone else, refunding the sponsor if it’s never delivered. Worth knowing if you’re sponsoring, not just if you’re contributing.

Payment links: the same idea packaged for reuse

A payment link is a payment request you can reuse — one URL, shared once (in a README, a project page, or a recurring invoice message), rather than freshly generated per delivery. It fits recurring work: a maintenance retainer, a support contract, or a “buy me a coffee”-style link for smaller, informal contributions. For one-off deliverables, a fresh payment request tied to that specific delivery is usually the clearer choice — the amount and description match exactly what was delivered.

Where the money actually goes: payout basics

Getting a payment request or bounty paid doesn’t put money directly in your bank account — it credits a balance you then withdraw. On Gitpay, that withdrawal is called a payout, and how it works depends on which payout method you have connected: a bank account through Stripe, an account on Whop, or a linked PayPal account. Card payments also don’t clear instantly — providers hold funds for a short settlement period (commonly a few days) before they’re available to withdraw. If you’re delivering software work regularly, it’s worth setting up your payout method before you need your first payment, not after.

If a payment is later disputed or refunded, that can be debited back out of your balance even after it was credited — see disputes and refunds if that happens to you.

Common mistakes

  • Sending the payment request separately from the handoff. Bundle them. Separate messages create a second thing the client can forget or deprioritize.
  • Starting work before being assigned or claimed. On a funded issue, this risks wasted work if someone else is already assigned, or if scope shifts after you started.
  • No clear “done” moment. If acceptance criteria are vague, payment becomes negotiable indefinitely. Tie the request to something concrete: a merged PR, a deployed feature, an agreed milestone.
  • Not setting up a payout method in advance. Discovering you have no active payout method the day you’re supposed to get paid adds an avoidable delay.
  • Treating a payment link as identical to an invoice. It removes payment friction; it doesn’t necessarily satisfy a client’s accounting or tax requirements. Ask if you’re unsure.

A short checklist for your next delivery

Whichever situation you’re in, before you consider the work “done”:

  1. What was delivered — one to three bullet points.
  2. Where it’s live or how to verify it (staging/production link, test steps).
  3. What’s next for the other side, if anything.
  4. The payment request, payment link, or (for a funded issue) the claim/PR link.

Where this fits on Gitpay

Gitpay connects both situations described above to the same underlying flow: fund an issue or send a payment request, deliver against it with a Pull Request or an explicit handoff, and get paid once it’s accepted.

  • Sponsoring or funding work: Funding issues
  • Delivering and claiming a bounty: Claims — claiming tasks and tracking transfers
  • Sending a payment request for service work: How our payment works
  • Getting your money out: How payouts work

If you want to try the workflow described here rather than just read about it, create a payment request or fund your next issue on Gitpay.
entry.summary: A practical workflow for getting paid after delivering code: use a payment request or a funded issue instead of chasing an invoice, whether you work freelance or on open source.
